definition: Data collected by an individual or group using their own resources. Generally the preferred data source, because you know exactly where it came from.
Data collected by a group directly from its own audience, then sold to another party.
Data collected by an outside source that did not collect it directly, often aggregated from a number of other sources. Can be useful but needs extra scrutiny for accuracy, bias, and credibility.
All possible data values that exist in a given dataset or group — every unit that could be measured, not just the ones actually measured.
A part of a population that is representative of the population as a whole, used when collecting data from an entire population is impractical.
Data organized in a specific format, such as rows and columns, that makes it easy to store, query, and export.

Data that isn't organized in any easily identifiable way, such as video, audio, social media content, or open-ended survey responses. Far more common in the world than structured data, and harder to search, manage, and analyze.
Data collected first-hand by the researcher using it, such as an interview or survey they conducted themselves.
Data gathered by other people or other research, such as a purchased customer dataset or government census data.
Data that lives inside a company's own systems, such as employee wages tracked by HR or a store's own sales figures.
Data that lives outside of a company or organization, such as national wage averages or a customer's credit report.
Data that is measured and can take almost any numeric value, such as height or temperature.
Data that is counted and has a limited number of possible values, such as the number of daily hospital visits or tickets sold.
A type of qualitative data whose categories have no set order, such as new customer, returning customer, or regular customer.
A type of qualitative data with a set order or scale, such as movie star ratings or income brackets.
The process of creating diagrams that visually represent how data is organized and structured, at a conceptual, logical, or physical level of detail.
sequence: Conceptual — high-level structure, no technical detail
Logical — technical relationships, attributes, and entities
Physical — actual table names, column names, and data types

definition: A specific kind of data attribute that tells what kind of value the data is — a number, a text/string, or a Boolean, in a typical spreadsheet.
One complete entry in a data table — the database and query-language term for what a spreadsheet calls a row.
One characteristic shared across every record in a table — the database and query-language term for what a spreadsheet calls a column. Every field holds a single data type.
The specific piece of data held in one field of one record — a single cell's worth of data.
A way of combining true/false conditions into a single filter using the operators AND (all conditions true), OR (at least one true), and NOT (excludes a condition).
A data format where each subject has a single row with multiple columns holding the values of its various attributes or time points. Easy to compare across columns.
A data format where each row is one time point for one subject, so a subject spans multiple rows. Stays compact as more variables are added.
The process of changing a dataset's format, structure, or values — adding, deleting, renaming, joining, or converting data to make it easier to use, merge, or move between systems.
A conscious or subconscious preference in favor of or against a person, group of people, or thing.
When a preference in favor of or against a person, group of people, or thing systematically skews data analysis results in a certain direction.
Overrepresenting or underrepresenting certain members of a population as a result of working with a sample that is not representative of the population as a whole.
The tendency to search for or interpret information in a way that confirms pre-existing beliefs.
The tendency for different people to observe the same thing differently.
The tendency to interpret an ambiguous situation in a positive or negative way based on expectation rather than evidence.
When the sample of the population being measured is representative of the population as a whole, typically achieved through random sampling.
A framework for judging whether a data source is trustworthy: reliable, original, comprehensive, current, and cited.
A data source that is reliable, original, comprehensive, current, and cited (ROCCC).
A data source that is not reliable, original, comprehensive, current, or cited (ROCCC) — and may contain human error or flat-out incorrect information.
The aspect of data ethics establishing that individuals own the raw data they provide, and retain primary control over how it's used and shared.
The aspect of data ethics presuming that all data-processing activities and algorithms should be explainable and understood by the individual who provides the data.
The aspect of data ethics presuming an individual's right to know how and why their personal data will be used before agreeing to provide it.
The aspect of data ethics presuming individuals should be aware of financial transactions resulting from the use of their personal data, and the scale of those transactions.
Preserving a data subject's information and activity any time a data transaction occurs, including their legal rights to access, inspect, correct, and consent to the use of their data.
A policy-making body in the European Union created to help protect people and their data.
The process of protecting people's private or sensitive data by eliminating identifying information — typically by blanking, hashing, or masking it.
Information that can be used, alone or combined with other data, to identify a specific person — names, phone numbers, addresses, social security numbers, and similar data.
A process used to wipe data clean of all personally identifying information, common in sensitive industries like healthcare and finance.
The aspect of data ethics that promotes the free access, usage, and sharing of data.
The ability of data systems and services to openly connect and share data with each other — a key factor in the successful use of open data among companies and governments.
A database that contains a series of related tables that can be connected via their relationships — one or more shared fields between tables.
An identifier that references a column in which each value is unique — a unique identifier for each record in a table. A table can have only one, and it can never be null or blank.
A field within a database table that is a primary key in another table, used to connect the two tables. A table can hold multiple foreign keys.
A primary key constructed from two or more columns of a table together, used when no single column is unique on its own.
A database in which only related data is stored in each table, connected through keys rather than duplicated — applied to eliminate redundancy, increase data integrity, and reduce complexity.
When the same piece of data is stored in two or more places.
Data about data — information that helps identify, interpret, and reuse a piece of data, such as its title, source, creation date, and structure.
Metadata that describes a piece of data and can be used to identify it at a later point in time, such as a title, tags, or categories.
Metadata that indicates how a piece of data is organized and whether it is part of one or more than one data collection.
Metadata that indicates the technical source of a digital asset, such as who created or last modified it and when.
A tabular inventory of a dataset's tables and their attributes/columns, including data types, sometimes supplemented with constraints or descriptions.
A database created to store metadata centrally, giving standardized information about where data lives across systems and how it connects.

A process for ensuring the formal management of a company's data assets, covering security, privacy, integrity, usability, and data flows, along with the roles and responsibilities of the people who maintain it.
A delimited plain-text file that uses a comma to separate values, one of the most portable formats for moving structured data between systems.
The section of a SQL query that indicates the subset of columns to return from a dataset.
The section of a SQL query that indicates where the selected data comes from.
The section of a SQL query that specifies criteria the requested data must meet.
A vendor-specific variation of SQL, such as BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server — mostly consistent, but differing on details like case sensitivity.
A naming style that separates words with underscores instead of spaces, used for SQL column names because spaces in a name will silently break a query.
Consistent guidelines that describe the content, creation date, and version of a file in its name.
Protecting data from unauthorized access or corruption by adopting safety measures.
Features such as password protection, user permissions, and encryption that are used to protect a spreadsheet or database.
A security measure that uses a unique algorithm to alter data and make it unusable to anyone without the "key" needed to reverse it.
A security measure that replaces protected data elements with randomly generated "tokens," while the original data is stored separately and mapped to those tokens.
